summary: Fixes a weakness in TLS where the master secret was not tied to the session details such as the server certificate. An active attacker could set up two sessions that share the same secret and then exploit session resumption or other authentication. This extension binds the secret to the handshake. It was replaced by RFC 9846.

eli5.summary: Two locks accidentally used the same key, so a trickster could swap between them. This makes each key unique to its own conversation. It was replaced by RFC 9846.

questions: what is the tls extended master secret
what is the tls triple handshake attack
how does extended master secret prevent attacks
why is the master secret important in tls
subtitle: Binding the TLS master secret to the full handshake to prevent secret synchronization attacks.

tldr.problem: The TLS master secret was not cryptographically bound to session details like the server certificate, allowing an attacker to set up two sessions that share the same secret and exploit session resumption or authentication mechanisms.
tldr.mechanism: This extension computes the master secret using a hash of the full handshake messages instead of just random values, ensuring each session gets a unique secret bound to its specific parameters.
tldr.outcome: The master secret becomes unique to each handshake context, preventing the triple handshake attack and similar man-in-the-middle attacks. RFC 9846 later replaced this extension.

today: RFC 9846 supersedes this extension with a more comprehensive update to TLS specifications.

sections.title: The Master Secret Problem
sections.content:
In TLS, the master secret is the root secret from which all session encryption keys are derived. It is computed from the pre-master secret (generated during key exchange) plus the client and server random values. The problem is that this formula does not depend on other session details like which certificates were presented or which ciphersuite was agreed upon.

An active attacker can exploit this by setting up two separate TLS sessions—one with the client and one with the legitimate server—such that both sessions compute the same master secret. The attacker can then transparently forward messages between the client and server while being able to read and modify them. This attack is especially dangerous because it defeats session resumption authentication and channel binding protections.
sections.eli5: The master secret is made from a secret number and two random numbers. But if an attacker can control both random numbers and the secret number, they can make two different conversations have the same secret.

sections.title: The Triple Handshake Attack
sections.content:
The triple handshake attack works in three stages. First, an attacker intercepts a client's connection to the legitimate server, forwarding the handshake messages while replacing the server's certificate with its own. Because the random values and key exchange are the same on both sides, both the client-to-attacker session and the attacker-to-server session end up with the same master secret.

Second, the attacker can abandon this position. The client and server, unaware of the man-in-the-middle, now possess the same session state. Third, when the client tries to resume the session (either explicitly or implicitly), the attacker can resume its own session with the server and forward the abbreviated handshake unchanged. Since the handshake log and keys are identical on both sides, protections based on the uniqueness of channel bindings or finish message verification fail.

This attack undermines mechanisms like secure renegotiation and application-level authentication that depend on the uniqueness of the master secret.
sections.eli5: An attacker sits between you and a server, copying everything you both do. Later, you try to reconnect to your server, but the attacker can replay those same messages between you and the server because they're identical.

sections.title: Session Hash and Extended Master Secret
sections.content:
The extension defines a session hash: a hash of all handshake messages from ClientHello through ClientKeyExchange. This hash captures the entire negotiation context, including the certificate presented, the ciphersuite chosen, and the key exchange parameters.

Instead of computing the master secret as PRF(pre_master_secret, "master secret", ClientHello.random + ServerHello.random), the extended master secret uses PRF(pre_master_secret, "extended master secret", session_hash). Because the session hash includes all handshake messages up to the key exchange, any difference in the handshake—such as different certificates or different ciphersuites—produces a different session hash and thus a different master secret.

This design ensures that two sessions can only have the same master secret if the attacker allows all handshake parameters to be identical on both sides, making the attack impossible in practice.
sections.eli5: Instead of using just two random numbers, we now use a fingerprint of the entire conversation up to that point. If anything is different between two conversations, their fingerprints are different, so the resulting key is different.

sections.title: Extension Negotiation
sections.content:
The extension uses extension type 0x0017 and has no extension data. Both client and server must explicitly support it. In a full handshake, if both ClientHello and ServerHello include the extension, the extended master secret derivation is used. Otherwise, the legacy computation applies.

For session resumption (abbreviated handshakes), the behavior is strict: if the original session used the extended master secret but the resumption attempt does not include the extension, the server MUST abort the handshake. Similarly, if the original session did not use the extension but the resumption attempt offers it, the server SHOULD continue with a full handshake instead.

Implementations that wish to support legacy clients and servers can choose to accept handshakes without the extension, but they must not use the resulting session for features like renegotiation, key export, or compound authentication, since those are vulnerable to the triple handshake attack without the extension.
sections.eli5: Both sides announce whether they support the new safety feature. If one side offers it but the other does not, they either both refuse (safest) or both fall back to the old way but do not use the keys for authentication.

sections.title: Security Guarantees
sections.content:
With the extended master secret extension, each session gets a unique master secret that is cryptographically bound to its full handshake context. This prevents unknown key-share attacks and thwarts the triple handshake attack at its first stage—the attacker can no longer force two different sessions to share a secret.

The extension recommends that hash functions used for the session hash be collision resistant. For TLS 1.2, which uses SHA-256 or better, this is satisfied. For earlier versions, the session hash uses the concatenation of MD5 and SHA1, mirroring the Finished message hash to inherit the same security guarantees.

One edge case exists: if new ciphersuites or extensions add handshake messages between ClientKeyExchange and Finished, those messages are not part of the session hash. Applications storing additional information in session tickets should be aware that the session hash does not cover them.
sections.eli5: With this protection, no two conversations can accidentally end up with the same secret unless they are identical in every way. And because the attack requires differences in certificates and ciphers, it becomes impossible.

viz.caption: Original vs. extended master secret computation

left.title: Original (vulnerable)
left.desc: Depends only on two random values, not on session parameters.

right.title: Extended (protected)
right.desc: Depends on the full handshake context, including certificates and ciphersuite.
